lead: AR and MR place computer-made objects into the real world and hold them in place while the user moves. This unit explains how that is done: the system blocks, the displays, the pose tracking, the software toolkits, the interaction and the applications. By the end you can size a latency or tracking budget, pick a display and a toolkit for a task, and say how you would evaluate the finished system.
about: This unit is about augmented and mixed reality: systems that add computer-made objects to the real world and keep them registered while the user moves. Chapter 6.1 gives the definition, the requirements and the system blocks. 6.2 shows the three ways a virtual image can reach the eye. 6.3 explains how the machine finds its own pose, from printed markers to SLAM. 6.4 surveys the software that packages this tracking work. 6.5 turns tracking into interaction: gaze, gesture, voice, travel and wayfinding. 6.6 shows where these systems are used and how they are judged. 6.7 looks at persistent shared worlds and what comes next. Each chapter leans on the earlier ones, so read in order.

chapters.idea: AR adds computer-made objects to the real world, keeps them fixed to real places, and does so live, so the three requirements are: combine real and virtual, register in 3D, and run in real time.
chapters.depth: Definition of augmented reality and how it differs from VR and MR. The reality-virtuality continuum (real, augmented reality, augmented virtuality, virtual reality) and where AR sits on it. The three requirements, stated as a test you can apply to any product. Features: 3D registration, real-time response, context awareness, hands-free use. The classic AR methods: see-through (optical and video), monitor-based and projection-based. System architecture as blocks: sensors and tracker produce a pose, a registration unit maps world points into camera coordinates, a renderer draws the virtual camera view, a combiner shows real and virtual light together, the user moves and closes the loop. The scene graph inside the AR application. Main challenges: latency, registration error, limited field of view, changing light, occlusion, battery and privacy. Some syllabi call this 'taxonomy of AR' or 'AR systems and functionality'.

figure.title: AR system blocks
figure.aria: Block diagram of an AR system: the real world is sensed, a pose is estimated, registration maps world points into the camera, the renderer draws the virtual view, the display merges it, and the moving user closes the loop.

chapters.example: A head tracker reports a new head angle every 50 ms. The user turns the head at 120 degrees per second. How far does the virtual overlay slip, and how fast would the system have to be to keep the slip under 5 mm at a 2 m viewing distance? Slip angle = 120 deg/s × 0.05 s = 6 degrees. Apparent shift = 2 m × tan 6° = 2 × 0.1051 = 0.21 m, that is 21 cm. For 5 mm at 2 m, tan θ = 0.005/2 = 0.0025, so θ = 0.143 degrees. Allowed delay = 0.143/120 = 0.0012 s, about 1.2 ms. No tracker is that fast, so the system must predict the pose forward, not only react to it.
chapters.trap: Saying AR is a camera picture with an image pasted on top. The marks come from the three requirements, and real-time 3D registration is the one that separates AR from a simple video overlay.
chapters.prereq: Unit 1: what VR, AR, MR and XR are, and the three I's.
chapters.leave: See-through optics to 6.2, tracking algorithms to 6.3, AR software to 6.4.

chapters.idea: The user must see the virtual object and the real world in one view, and there are only three routes: let real light pass through a combiner, mix camera pictures on a screen, or project light straight onto the real surface.
chapters.depth: Optical see-through: a half-silvered mirror or a waveguide combiner reflects the microdisplay image into the eye while real light passes through; real view has no camera delay, but brightness drops, the virtual image sits at a fixed distance, and the eye is offset from the display optics. Video see-through: a camera captures the real view, the renderer composites virtual objects into that image, and a screen shows one combined picture; latency can be matched between the two streams, occlusion can be drawn, but the camera is offset from the eye (parallax) and the camera adds delay. Monitor-based (desktop) AR. Projection-based AR: a projector throws light onto the real object, fixed (spatial AR) or handheld; no eyewear is needed, but the user can block the beam and surfaces must be light-coloured. Comparison table on latency, brightness, field of view, resolution, occlusion, safety, cost. The vergence-accommodation problem stated in one paragraph. Phone AR as video see-through on a hand-held screen. Some syllabi call this 'optical see-through and video see-through displays'.

figure.aria: Tree of AR display types: see-through splits into optical and video, projection splits into spatial and handheld, and monitor-based sits beside them.

chapters.example: A video see-through headset needs 33 ms to capture a frame at 30 frames per second, 20 ms to compute the pose and 15 ms to show the frame. An optical see-through unit adds only 20 ms of tracking and display delay. The user turns the head at 60 degrees per second. Find the misregistration angle and the apparent shift at 1.5 m. Video path: 33 + 20 + 15 = 68 ms, angle = 60 × 0.068 = 4.08 degrees, shift = 1.5 × tan 4.08° = 1.5 × 0.0713 = 0.107 m, about 10.7 cm. Optical path: 20 ms, angle = 1.2 degrees, shift = 1.5 × 0.02095 = 0.031 m, about 3.1 cm. The video path is about 3.4 times worse here, and matched-latency compositing is what a designer must add to fix it.
chapters.trap: Writing that video see-through is simply better, or swapping the two. Keep the fixed trade: optical keeps the real view bright and true but cannot hide real objects; video can draw occlusion but adds camera delay and camera-eye parallax.
chapters.prereq: 6.1; Unit 3 for head-mounted and stereoscopic displays; Unit 2 for head tracking.
chapters.leave: Head-mounted optics and stereoscopy in detail to Unit 3; pose estimation to 6.3.

chapters.idea: Registration needs the camera pose in every frame, and the three families trade how much world knowledge they assume: a printed marker, natural image features, or a map built while the camera moves (SLAM).
chapters.depth: Pose means 6 degrees of freedom: 3 position values and 3 orientation values. Marker-based tracking: fiducial patterns (black square with a white border and an inner code), detection pipeline of grayscale, threshold, contour, four corners, homography, code check, pose from homography, and a temporal filter to smooth jitter. Marker size and camera focal length set the usable range and the pose noise. Markerless tracking: corner and blob feature detectors, descriptors, matching with an outlier test, homography for a plane, PnP for a known 3D model, RANSAC to reject wrong matches. Model-based tracking of a known object. SLAM: front-end tracking of features, the map, back-end optimisation, loop closure, relocalisation after tracking loss; visual-inertial odometry that fuses camera and IMU; monocular scale ambiguity; drift over distance and how anchors reduce it. Only a few universities teach SLAM at this depth, so keep to the pipeline and the ideas, not the optimisation mathematics.

figure.title: Marker tracking pipeline
figure.aria: Pipeline of a marker-based tracker: each camera frame is thresholded, the marker corners are found, the code is decoded, and the homography gives the pose used to draw the overlay.

chapters.example: A square marker has a side of 80 mm. It appears 160 pixels wide in a camera with focal length 800 pixels. Find the distance. Then find the distance error if a corner is located to within 1 pixel. Depth Z = f × W / w = 800 × 0.08 / 160 = 0.4 m. The relative width error is 1/160 = 0.00625, so the depth error is 0.4 × 0.00625 = 0.0025 m, that is 2.5 mm. If the user walks to 0.2 m, the marker covers 320 pixels, the relative error halves to 0.003125, and the depth error falls to 0.2 × 0.003125 = 0.6 mm. This is why markers are tracked close and why apparent size sets both range and accuracy.
chapters.trap: Saying SLAM reports a metric world pose. With one camera the map has no absolute scale. Also forgetting that marker tracking needs camera calibration: without focal length and lens distortion values the pose is wrong no matter how clean the detection.
chapters.prereq: Unit 2 for trackers and sensors; Unit 4 for transformation matrices and yaw, pitch, roll; 6.1.
chapters.leave: Bundle adjustment and filter mathematics; general sensor description to Unit 2.

chapters.idea: An AR toolkit turns tracking into a software call: you declare a target or an anchor and the toolkit returns a pose every frame, so toolkits differ in what they track and which devices they run on.
chapters.depth: ARToolKit: open-source C library, printed patterns, the ancestor of marker tracking, needs a camera calibration file. Vuforia: image targets, multi-targets, cylinder targets, model targets, ground plane, device database against cloud database, Unity extension, runs on many phones. ARCore: Android, motion tracking by visual-inertial odometry, environmental understanding through feature points and planes, light estimation, depth, anchors, geospatial placement. ARKit: iOS and iPadOS, world tracking, plane and mesh understanding, image and object detection, face tracking, people occlusion, scene reconstruction. A comparison table on platform, what it tracks, marker support, plane detection, occlusion and licence. The content tools around the SDK: Unity or Unreal to render, Blender, Maya or 3ds Max to model, texture and bake light; the export path from model to engine to SDK to device. Note for exam wording: this chapter is a tool survey, not a build manual.

figure.title: AR content pipeline
figure.aria: Content pipeline for an AR app: a model is made in Blender, imported to Unity, placed using the pose from an AR SDK, fixed with an anchor, and built onto a phone.

chapters.example: A Unity AR app must hold 60 frames per second on a mid-range phone, so each frame has 1/60 = 16.7 ms. The developer sets this budget: tracking 6 ms, rendering 8 ms, UI and app logic 1.5 ms. Sum = 15.5 ms, leaving 1.2 ms of headroom. In a dark corridor the tracker drops many features and its cost rises to 9 ms, so the sum becomes 18.5 ms and the frame rate falls to 1/0.0185 = 54 frames per second, below the target. The fix is to lower the render cost, for example by cutting the number of draw calls, until the sum returns under 16.7 ms.
chapters.trap: Treating Vuforia, ARCore and ARKit as three versions of one product. Vuforia is a marker and image-target SDK that runs on many devices; ARCore and ARKit are platform tracking engines tied to Android and iOS hardware. Also ARCore is not a renderer: Unity does the drawing.
chapters.prereq: 6.1 to 6.3; Unit 5 for game engines, scene graphs and Unity scripting.
chapters.leave: Unity C# scripting and scene graphs to Unit 5; modelling and the rendering pipeline to Unit 4; the application areas to 6.6.

chapters.idea: With no keyboard or mouse, mixed reality interaction is built from gaze, hand gestures, voice and controllers, and every action must be recognised, confirmed and answered with feedback inside a frame or two.
chapters.depth: The input set: 6-DoF controllers, hand tracking with joint poses, pinch and grab, eye gaze, voice, and real surfaces as controls. The four interaction tasks applied to MR: selection, manipulation, navigation or travel, and system control. Near interaction (touching a hologram) against far interaction (a ray from the hand). Gaze-and-commit: look to aim, pinch or say 'select' to fire. Gesture set design rules: few gestures, easy to hold, visually distinct, no long holds, no raised-arm fatigue ('gorilla arm'). Feedback: hover highlight, sound, haptics, and a visible confirmation. Placing and anchoring content on mapped real surfaces. Navigation in MR: walking, teleport, world-in-miniature, portals, floor arrows. Wayfinding support: landmarks, route preview, minimap, turn-by-turn arrows on the floor. Multimodal commands and why two channels cut errors. Evaluation measures: task time, error rate, selection accuracy, comfort, workload score.

figure.title: MR interaction loop
figure.aria: Interaction loop for mixed reality: the user's gaze, pinch or voice is sensed, recognised, given a confidence, turned into a system response, and answered with visual, audio or haptic feedback.

chapters.example: A gesture recogniser is tested with two gestures, pinch and grab, 50 trials each. Of the 50 pinch trials, 46 are called pinch, 3 are called grab and 1 is missed. Of the 50 grab trials, 45 are called grab and 4 are called pinch. Find accuracy, and the precision and recall of pinch. Accuracy = (46 + 45)/100 = 91%. Pinch precision = 46/(46 + 4) = 92%, because 4 grab trials were wrongly called pinch. Pinch recall = 46/50 = 92%. Both mistakes cost the user a wrong action, so a designer raises the confidence threshold for pinch and adds a hover highlight before commit.
chapters.trap: Mixing up travel, wayfinding and manipulation. Travel moves the viewpoint, wayfinding is knowing where to go, manipulation moves the object. Also do not copy fixed-distance desktop menus onto a head-worn display.
chapters.prereq: Unit 5 for manipulation, travel, wayfinding and system control; Unit 2 for gesture interfaces and hand tracking; 6.2 for the display.
chapters.leave: General 3D interaction theory and menu design to Unit 5; haptic device hardware to Unit 3.

chapters.idea: AR earns its cost where the information belongs to a place or an object: a patient on the table, a machine on the line, a page in a book, a street in front of you.
chapters.depth: Medicine: surgical navigation with pre-operative scans registered to the patient, vein finding, rehabilitation games, anatomy teaching, remote mentoring during an operation. Education: AR books and 3D models, chemistry and anatomy, museum and historic-site walkthroughs, laboratory and safety training, and the evidence for learning gains with its small samples. Entertainment: location-based games, camera and face filters, live sports graphics, stage and theme-park effects. Industry: assembly and service instructions, remote expert help, warehouse picking, inspection and quality checks, training without stopping the line. Mention retail, defence and navigation briefly. A use-case template you can answer with: what is tracked, what is drawn, which display type, which device, how it is evaluated. Costs and limits: device cost, content authoring time, hygiene, user comfort, distraction and safety.

figure.aria: Tree of AR application areas with three example uses under each of medicine, education, entertainment and industry.

chapters.example: Suppose 60 students are split into 30 using an AR anatomy app and 30 using printed notes. Both groups score a pre-test mean of 40 out of 100. The post-test mean is 78 for the AR group and 66 for the control group. Find the normalised gain. Gain = (post - pre)/(100 - pre). AR group: (78 - 40)/(100 - 40) = 38/60 = 0.63. Control group: (66 - 40)/60 = 26/60 = 0.43. The raw improvement is 38 points against 26 points. With only 30 students per group this is a signal, not proof: random assignment, the same teacher and a blinded marking scheme are needed before you claim a learning gain.
chapters.trap: Answering with a list of app names. The marks are for what is tracked, what is drawn, which display is used, and how the system was evaluated.
chapters.leave: Tool-specific build steps to 6.4; what happens to these areas next to 6.7.

chapters.idea: The metaverse is the persistent, shared, synchronous 3D layer over the internet, and XR trends are the hardware and network steps that make it wearable and always on.
chapters.depth: Definition through its properties: persistence, synchrony, a shared space, avatars, an economy, and interoperability between devices. The layer model from hardware up to experience. The AR cloud and spatial anchors as the way two devices agree on the same real point. Edge and cloud rendering, and the latency of 5G and Wi-Fi links. WebXR in the browser. Digital twins. AI-generated avatars, speech and content. Hardware trends: waveguide glasses, micro-LED and laser scanning, pancake optics, colour passthrough mixed reality, eye and hand tracking, SLAM on the device itself. Standards: OpenXR for the application interface, glTF and USDZ for content. Challenges: privacy with always-on cameras, safety, cost, energy, accessibility, content moderation and the digital divide. A realistic near-term view: phone AR and light glasses for guidance, not the replacement of every screen.

figure.aria: Layered stack of the metaverse, from devices and network at the base up through standards, engine and platform to the user's experience.

chapters.example: A cloud-rendered XR system allows 20 ms from head motion to the photon leaving the display. Rendering takes 8 ms and the display scan takes 4 ms, leaving 8 ms for the network. Light in fibre travels at about 2 × 10⁸ m per second. A round trip of 8 ms covers 8 × 10⁻³ × 2 × 10⁸ = 1.6 × 10⁶ m, that is 1600 km, so the server can be at most 800 km away one way. With a server 1000 km away the round trip is 2000 km = 2 × 10⁶ m and costs 10 ms, total 10 + 8 + 4 = 22 ms, which misses the budget. This is why cloud rendering pushes the server to the network edge.
chapters.trap: Calling any VR app or game 'the metaverse'. A metaverse needs persistence and shared state across users and devices. Also do not give a date for full AR glasses or promise features that no shipping product has.
chapters.prereq: 6.1 to 6.6, and Unit 1 for the XR definitions.
chapters.leave: Display optics to 6.2; tracking to 6.3; networking protocol detail is outside this unit.
